Abstract Paleomagnetic investigations of the Iranian-Afghanian Plate -- well defined by geo- logical history and seismotectonics yield following pole positions: Permian 42W 8 N, lower Cretaceous 48 W 65 N, lower Tertiary 100 W 75 N, upper Tertiary 180 W 78 N. These paleomagnetic results, supported by fracture zones and magnetic anomalies of the Indian Ocean floor make it possible to reconstruct the plate movement from the eastern margin of Gondwana to the southern margin of Laurasia. After the prepermian sep- aration from Gondwana the Afghan-Iranian Plate moves northward rotating anticlockwise and collides with the Russian Plate until lower Cretaceous time. Earlier than lower Tertiary the Arabian Plate reaches at the SW margin of the Afghan-Iranian Plate. The Indian Plate, moving forward from SE pushes the Afghan continental crust in northward direction since upper Tertiary time. The collisions are marked by folding

J. D. A. Piper, Sub-department of Geophysics, Oliver Lodge Laboratory, University of Liverpool, Oxford Street, Liverpool L69 3BX, England. April 16th, 1976. The Precambrian Ilimaussaq complex is one of a number of peralkaline instrusions within the Gardar igneous province of south Green­ land, but is unique in the high degree of peralkalinity and enrichment in such elements as Zr and Cl. This paper reports palaeomagnetic results from a collection of syenites from the margin and agpaites (highly undersaturated· syenites) from the interior of the pluton. Such a study has become particularly relevant in the light of detailed geochronological work on the com­ plex by Moorbath et al. (1960) and Blaxland et al. (1976). Geology The geology of the Ilimaussaq intrusion is described in a comprehensive memoir by Us­ sing (1912), and more recent accounts include those by Ferguson (1964, 1970), Hamilton (1964), Ss,Srensen et al. (1969) and Bohse et al. (1971); these descriptions reference many other more specialised studies of the complex. Th.e earliest phase is a

d more recent accounts include those by Ferguson (1964, 1970), Hamilton (1964), Ss,Srensen et al. (1969) and Bohse et al. (1971); these descriptions reference many other more specialised studies of the complex. Th.e earliest phase is an augite syenite which forms a marginal envelope around the side of the intrusion at its southern margin and also 7 D.g.F. 25 occurs at the uppermost levels. The bulk of this unit is medium to coarse grained but includes a chilled facies at the margin; ne­ pheline occurs further from the contact with the country rock and local mineral banding with steep inward dips is also observed. Palaeomagnetic sites 5, 4, 3, 2, 1 comprise a single traverse across the syenite beginning near the contact with country rocks on the east side of Kangerdluarssuak; site 6 is close to the contact on west side of the fjord (fig. 1). Within the intrusion, rhythmically layered kakortokites (eudialyte-bearing nepheline syen­ ites) represent the deepest exposed part of the intrusion, and Bohse et al. (1971) have recog­ nised and mapped 29 major layers comprising arfvedsonite, eudialyte and feldspar with nepheline. J. D. A. Piper, Sub-department of Geophysics, Oliver Lodge Laboratory, University of Liverpool, Oxford Street, Liverpool L69 3BX, England. April 16th, 1976. The Precambrian Ilimaussaq complex is one of a number of peralkaline instrusions within the Gardar igneous province of south Green­ land, but is unique in the high degree of peralkalinity and enrichment in such elements as Zr and Cl. This paper reports palaeomagnetic results from a collection of syenites from the margin and agpaites (highly undersaturated· syenites) from the interior of the pluton. Such a study has become particularly relevant in the light of detailed geochronological work on the com­ plex by Moorbath et al. (1960) and Blaxland et al. (1976). Geology The geology of the Ilimaussaq intrusion is described in a comprehensive memoir by Us­ sing (1912), and more recent accounts include those by Ferguson (1964, 1970), Hamilton (1964), Ss,Srensen et al. (1969) and Bohse et al. (1971); these descriptions reference many other more specialised studies of the complex. Th.e earliest phase is a

(1971); these descriptions reference many other more specialised studies of the complex. Th.e earliest phase is an augite syenite which forms a marginal envelope around the side of the intrusion at its southern margin and also 7 D.g.F. 25 occurs at the uppermost levels. The bulk of this unit is medium to coarse grained but includes a chilled facies at the margin; ne­ pheline occurs further from the contact with the country rock and local mineral banding with steep inward dips is also observed. Palaeomagnetic sites 5, 4, 3, 2, 1 comprise a single traverse across the syenite beginning near the contact with country rocks on the east side of Kangerdluarssuak; site 6 is close to the contact on west side of the fjord (fig. 1). Within the intrusion, rhythmically layered kakortokites (eudialyte-bearing nepheline syen­ ites) represent the deepest exposed part of the intrusion, and Bohse et al. (1971) have recog­ nised and mapped 29 major layers comprising arfvedsonite, eudialyte and feldspar with nepheline. a stable secondary magnetic moment and arguments are given for believing this to have been recently acquired. It therefore follows that haematite is more mobile in permeable sandstones than has generally been thought. The results suggest that the Jurassic palaeomagnetic pole for North America, based largely on preliminary work by Runcorn and Collinson & Runcorn from the same formation and similar red-bed lithologies, is based on rocks with a present-day component of magnetization. The virtual poles reported by DeBoer or Helsley & Steiner may be the best representations of the North American Jurassic palaeomagnetic pole position. A petrographic study indicates that the investigation of the Navajo Sandstone as a means of detailing the behaviour and detailing a part of the polar wandering curve for North America is not feasible. However, a residuum of the original Jurassic component may be seen in the reversely magnetized sites. There probably exist similar residue in the normally magnetized sites, but these Jurassic residues are much less clearly defined. Many others (Folk 1951; Correns 1950; Waldschmidt 1941) suggest similar sequences. Since this sequence is present in these red beds, a time relationship for the introduction of the haematite may be deduced. The distribution of the haematite staining, although not indicative of primary or secondary origin, is sufficient for placing some time limits on its introduction. Since haematite is present beneath the secondary overgrowths and at some sutured contacts, some haematite must have been present in these rocks during early diagenesis. These pole positions are com- pletely different from comparable pole positions for southeast Sicily and Africa and imply a clockwise rotation of west Sicily since the Upper Cretaceous of about 90 ° relative to southeast Sicily and Africa and also a clockwise rotation of about 60 ° relative to "stable" Europe. The sense of rotation of west Sicily is opposite to any known rotation of other crustal blocks in the central Mediterranean. 1. An analysis,of paleomagnetic remanence data shows that two units within the St. Joseph Till were sampled, although it has not been possible to find a consistent stratigraphic break from field examinations. These two units give separate virtual geomagnetic pole (VGP) positions of lat. 67.1" N, long. 297.8" W and lat. 65. lo N, long. 220.6" W. Remanence data from varved clays for the Walkerton area, which were deposited at about the same time as the St. Joseph Till, gave a VGP position close to the mean of all remanence results from the St. Joseph Till. s the St. Joseph Till, gave a VGP position close to the mean of all remanence results from the St. Joseph Till. A spruce log extracted from the till was dated at 13 100 -c 110 y B.P. (GSC-2213), which is consistent with the time of the Port Huron ice advance. Granulometric analysis, carbonate analysis, and pebble analysis showed variations which are directly related to the nature of the underlying bedrock and could not be used to differentiate the two till units. Ratios of purple (dark red) to white (light red) garnets also demonstrate the presence of two till units within the St. Joseph Till and thus support the interpretation of the remanence data. The results show that in the absence of direct field evidence remanence data is a sensitive tool which can be used to determine if more than one till unit is present. (GSC-2213), which is consistent with the time of the Port Huron ice advance. Granulometric analysis, carbonate analysis, and pebble analysis showed variations which are directly related to the nature of the underlying bedrock and could not be used to differentiate the two till units. Sampling was carried out using a field coring drill (Doell and Cox 1967) with which 3 to 7 cores per flow were drilled (because of difficulty in drilling, three flows in the Castles section are represented by less than 3 cores). Cores were oriented using a sun compass wherever possible and by sighting on geographic features whose true bearing had been determined using the sun and topographic maps. Measurements were done on a 5 Hz spinner magnetometer (Foster 1966). Alternating field demagnetization studies were carried out using magnetic cleaning apparatus similar to that described by McElhinny (1966). Detailed stepwise a.f. cleaning up to more than 2000 Oe was done on 24 pilot specimens from 13 of the Wait Creek flows. All specimens showed good end-points below 380 Oe peak a.f. ; the relative change in intensity at this field, JIJ,, was between 0.3 and 0.8 (Fig. 2). Either the number of field excur- sions occurring in the time period sampled was very high (or perhaps very local), or the results were due to fortuitous sampling, the probability of which is very low. The latter case is, however, intuitively more appealing. Since the age of the Wrangell Volcanics is near the Gilbert Reversed-Gauss Normal Epoch boundary, the geomagnetic field behavior re- corded may have occurred during polarity transi- tions. Earth Sci., 13,547-554 (1976) Introduction Knowledge of the temporal behavior of the geomagnetic field of the earth over time scales short compared to rates of polar wandering or continental drift is important in placing boun- dary conditions or limits on geomagnetic field models. Time-varying features of the geomag- netic field of interest that have been studied are reversals, intensities, secular variation, and field excursions. In order to investigate these aspects of the geomagnetic field at a remote time in the geo- logic past it is necessary to sample the paleo- magnetic field across a section of rock known to have been deposited and/or to have acquired a magnetic remanence more or less uniformly at a known rate. It intrudes Archean granitic and supracrustal rocks of the Slave Structural Province. Martineau and Lam- bert (1974) have shown that the northeastern part consists of silica-saturated layered diorites and gabbros intruded by magnetite-rich pyroxenites and a syenite ring dike (Fig. 2). The rest of the complex comprises silica-saturated and over- saturated syenites, and undersaturated foyaites and ijolites, which we refer to collectively as 'syenites'. There are local swarms of thin basic dikes and a carbonatite plug. Fenites are well developed about the margins of the silica-under- saturated rocks, and gas explosion vents with related breccias also occur near contacts. Earth Sci.. 13.476489(1976) Introduction Polyphase magnetization is the phenomenon whereby a rock unit may contain several different magnetizations, each corresponding to the geo- magnetic field at various times during the history of the rock unit. These magnetizations may be present in different oxide phases, or in different grain-size ranges of the same oxide phase. They can be separated by chemical leaching, which progressively removes the finer grain-size frac- tions and the magnetizations they carry; by al- ternating field (AF) demagnetization, which pro- gressively removes the magnetizations of lower remanent coercive force; or by thermal demag- netization, which progressively removes the magnetizations with lower blocking tempera- tures. The phenomenon of polyphase magnetiza- tion is analogous to polyphase deformation in metamorphic rocks, which is indicative of a complex metamorphic history, and to the occur- rence of a spread of apparent dates obtained in geochronological studies, which is indicative of a complex thermal history. In this paper we describe an instance ofpolyphase magnetization in unmetamorphosed igneous rocks. Geology The Big Spruce Complex occurs about 140 km northwest of Yellowknife (Fig. 1). It intrudes Archean granitic and supracrustal rocks of the Slave Structural Province. Martineau and Lam- bert (1974) have shown that the northeastern part consists of silica-saturated layered diorites and gabbros intruded by magnetite-rich pyroxenites and a syenite ring dike (Fig. 2). The rest of the complex comprises silica-saturated and over- saturated syenites, and undersaturated foyaites and ijolites, which we refer to collectively as 'syenites'. There are local swarms of thin basic dikes and a carbonatite plug. Fenites are well developed about the margins of the silica-under- saturated rocks, and gas explosion vents with related breccias also occur near contacts. The intrusion is cut by a small fault, and there is some indication from the regional geology that it lies in a major fault zone. The rocks commonly show internal fracturing, but there is no evi

These magnetizations may be present in different oxide phases, or in different grain-size ranges of the same oxide phase. They can be separated by chemical leaching, which progressively removes the finer grain-size frac- tions and the magnetizations they carry; by al- ternating field (AF) demagnetization, which pro- gressively removes the magnetizations of lower remanent coercive force; or by thermal demag- netization, which progressively removes the magnetizations with lower blocking tempera- tures. It intrudes Archean granitic and supracrustal rocks of the Slave Structural Province. The Big Spruce alkaline complex has yielded a Rb-Sr isochron of 21 11 + 40 m. y. The rocks are unmetamorphosed, but the local geochrono1ogical evidence indicates that they have had a complicated thermal history. The complex has four magnetizations, which can be separated by a two-stage demagnetization procedure. The D magnetization (19 sites; 022, +88; %, =So; pole 67" N 113" W) is considered to have been acquired at the time of emplacement because it generally has the highest blocking temperatures (500 to 650 "C). The X, Y, and Z magnetizations are believed to be later overprints, as they generally have lower blocking temperatures and have directions that are comparable to those found in younger rocks in the interval of approximately 2000 to 1400 m.y. Earth Sci.. 13.476489(1976) Introduction Polyphase magnetization is the phenomenon whereby a rock unit may contain several different magnetizations, each corresponding to the geo- magnetic field at various times during the history of the rock unit. These magnetizations may be present in different oxide phases, or in different grain-size ranges of the same oxide phase. They can be separated by chemical leaching, which progressively removes the finer grain-size frac- tions and the magnetizations they carry; by al- ternating field (AF) demagnetization, which pro- gressively removes the magnetizations of lower remanent coercive force; or by thermal demag- netization, which progressively removes the magnetizations with lower blocking tempera- tures. The phenomenon of polyphase magnetiza- tion is analogous to polyphase deformation in metamorphic rocks, which is indicative of a complex metamorphic history, and to the occur- rence of a spread of apparent dates obtained in geochronological studies, which is indicative of a complex thermal history. One of the simplest situations in paleomag- netism is that in which there is a primary mag- 'Earth Physics Branch Contribution No. 588.

Some of these data update previous preliminary results, while others provide new information. In some instances the original remanence direction has been obscured by subsequent remagnetization. Although magnetic inclinations of the Ordovician results are mostly shallower than contem-

d from the Mweel- rea ignimbrites of Killary Harbour, although internally consistent, do not conform to the locally inferred Ordovician geomagnetic field as based on English data (Deutsch and Somayajulu 1970; Morris et al. 1973). Other reported results from Ireland are either based on limited stability criteria, small collections, or give directions sug- gestive of remagnetization, and hence are of limited use. In this paper, a preliminary study previously reported from the Salrock intrusives is updated in the light of further sampling and laboratory treatment. Also, from the South Mayo Trough, new data are reported from two felsites that outcrop along its eastern margin. Excluding the data from Connemara, the only other Lower Paleozoic data from Ireland are the preliminary poles from the Ordovician inliers of Counties Louth, Meath, and Kildare (Morris and Robinson 1971). Also, from the South Mayo Trough, new data are reported from two felsites that outcrop along its eastern margin. Excluding the data from Connemara, the only other Lower Paleozoic data from Ireland are the preliminary poles from the Ordovician inliers of Counties Louth, Meath, and Kildare (Morris and Robinson 1971). Extensive resampling of the two inliers at Kildare and Portrane, together with new collections from Balbriggan and Grangegeeth, provide a better estimate of the local Ordovician remanence direction. All remanence measurements were made on a PAR-SM2D magnetometer. AF demagnetiza- tion was used to isolate the direction considered representative of the geomagnetic field at the time of rock formation. In this paper, results are presented from two regions in Ireland that are considered to have lain on opposite margins of the proposed ocean (Dewey 1969). Geologically, the ocean is considered to have reached maximum extent during the early Ordo- vician. Hence, comparison of Ordovician paleo- magnetic data from these two regions should provide an estimate of continental separation for this segment of the Caledonide belt. Data pertaining to this discussion are: the Chair of Kildare and the Grangegeeth Volcanics from eastern Ireland, and the Glensaul 'felsite' and Mweelrea ignimbrite from the South Mayo Trough in the west of Ireland. Other reported results from Ireland are either based on limited stability criteria, small collections, or give directions sug- gestive of remagnetization, and hence are of limited use. In this paper, a preliminary study previously reported from the Salrock intrusives is updated in the light of further sampling and laboratory treatment. Also, from the South Mayo Trough, new data are reported from two felsites that outcrop along its eastern margin. Excluding the data from Connemara, the only other Lower Paleozoic data from Ireland are the preliminary poles from the Ordovician inliers of Counties Louth, Meath, and Kildare (Morris and Robinson 1971). Extensive resampling of the two inliers at Kildare and Portrane, together with new collections from Balbriggan and Grangegeeth, provide a better estimate of the local Ordovician remanence direction. The Keuper Marl would have been better named Keuper Mudstone for it is only slightly calcareous consisting of a fine silt with an admixture of clay minerals and small dolomite crystals. In many places it is structureless, closely resembling loess but at Sidmouth it is stratified at some levels probably due to deposition in temporary lakes. When samples of this deposit are broken up a black ferromagnetic content can be separated. X-ray analysis shows this to be mostly haematite. The red cement may similarly be shown to be haematite. 2. A paleomagnetic survey (34 sites, 200 core samples) of an Archean greenstone belt just north of the Grenville Front is described. Sixty per cent of the samples have blocking tem- peratures less than 400°C and remanent coercive forces predominantly below 100 Oe, and they provide no information about the Precambrian geomagnetic field. The other samples contain many magnetizations of which two (CS and CH) can be clearly recognized. The CS magnetization occurs in basic sills, and has high blocking temperature (550 to 650°C) and remanent coercive force (often exceeding 1000 Oe) and a direction (186°,--38 °) that is not significantly different from that in Matachewan diabase dikes (2690 m.y.). CS is thought to have been caused by uplift following the Kenoran orogeny and its age is prob- ably about 2600 m.y. No older magnetization has been found. The CH magnetization occurs in several different bodies and has a direction (119 °, +51 °) similar to that observed in rocks from other places close to the Grenville Front. CH has more variable blocking temperatures (200 to 650°C) and remanent coercive forces (200 to > 1000 Oe) and is con- sidered to have been acquired by heating during uplift of the highly metamorphose Gren- ville Province to the south. Uplift occurred about I000 m.y. ago, and the CH magnetiza- tion is considered to be of this age. Evidence is presented to support the suggestion that there was an extensive magnetization episode both within and adjacent to the Grenville Province at that time. he Chibougamau rocks probably occurred soon after formation. The area is a general synclinorium, comprising two synclines separated by an anticline (Fig.4). Folding is steep, the dips of sills are commonly 60 ° or more, and they are occasionally overturned. PALEOMAGNETIC RESULTS Samples were collected from 34 sites. Five cores were obtained at each site, and two specimens were cut from each core. Remanent magnetization was measured by a Schonstedt SM1 spinner magnetometer. Thermal and alter- nating field (a.f.) demagnetization was carried out in quasi-zero field (< 2~) using the apparatus described by Roy et al. (1969, 1971, 1973). Thermal demagnetization has been carried out on 25 specimens and the decay curves are of four types (A--D in Fig.5). The A-type curves are square- shouldered, and the blocking temperatures range from 550 to 650 ° C. Iron oxides of the A-type specimens observed in polished sections are hematite, magnetite, and ilmenite. The gneissic rock at site 66 within the Grenville Province has blocking temperatures about 650 ° C, and contains rod-shaped hematite which is a recrystallization product. DISCUSSION We now consider the CH magnetization and kindred magnetizations found elsewhere. At Chibougamau CH occurs in Archean rocks north of the Gren- ville Front, and also in high-grade gneisses immediately south of the Front (site 66, Fig.4). The same magnetization direction occurs elsewhere both in- side, and marginal to, the Grenville Province. Inside the province it is charac- teristic of rocks whose remanence is due to magnetite (Whitestone anortho- 312 site XY magnetization, Morin anorthosite M, and the St. Urbain anorthosite SU, see Figs.1 and 7). Marginal to the province it has been found both at the Front itself (Grenville Front anorthosites GA) and immediately north of the Front (Michael gabbros MG, igneous rocks of the Seal and Croteau Groups SC2, and the Shabogamo gabbros SG2). Sixty per cent of the samples have blocking tem- peratures less than 400°C and remanent coercive forces predominantly below 100 Oe, and they provide no information about the Precambrian geomagnetic field. The other samples contain many magnetizations of which two (CS and CH) can be clearly recognized. The CS magnetization occurs in basic sills, and has high blocking temperature (550 to 650°C) and remanent coercive force (often exceeding 1000 Oe) and a direction (186°,--38 °) that is not significantly different from that in Matachewan diabase dikes (2690 m.y.). CH has more variable blocking temperatures (200 to 650°C) and remanent coercive forces (200 to > 1000 Oe) and is con- sidered to have been acquired by heating during uplift of the highly metamorphose Gren- ville Province to the south. THE LEWISIAN of north-west Scotland is a metamorphic complex composed mainly of banded gneisses but incorporating dykes, pegmafites and granite sheets as minor intrusive constituents. Three zones (Fig. I) have been recognized on the mainland (Peach et al. 19o7, Sutton & Watson 1951 ). The Central Zone consists primarily of gneisses in the granulite facies formed during the Scourian meta- morphism; in the Northern and Southern Zones the gneisses were reworked in amphibolite facies in the Laxfordian metamorphism. THE LEWISIAN of north-west Scotland is a metamorphic complex composed mainly of banded gneisses but incorporating dykes, pegmafites and granite sheets as minor intrusive constituents. Three zones (Fig. I) have been recognized on the mainland (Peach et al. 19o7, Sutton & Watson 1951 ). The Central Zone consists primarily of gneisses in the granulite facies formed during the Scourian meta- morphism; in the Northern and Southern Zones the gneisses were reworked in amphibolite facies in the Laxfordian metamorphism. These zones were origi- nally established with the aid of the dykes which are often undeformed and only slightly metamorphosed in the Central Zone but profoundly altered elsewhere. Both the Scourian and Laxfordian are now regarded as polyphase episodes re- sponsible for repeated heating and deformation. The significance and sta- bility of the different formations investigated in this study are demonstrated by the departure of the site NRM directions from the recent Earth's field direction (3310, 790N) and the evidence for reversal(s). 10. Curie Temperatures Thermomagnetic curves were obtained on 10 mg of powdered rock samples using a recording electromagnetic microbalance. Most of the curves obtained are relatively simple and indicate the presence of a single magnetic mineral having Curie temperature in the 5600-5900C temperature range; these data suggest that the magnetic mineral is almost pure magnetite. In a few samples, low temper- ature Curie points suggest the presence of small quantities of hemo-ilmenite. 11. Time (Age) and Origin of Magnetization The meaning of radiogenic age determinations, particularly of Precambrian rocks, is difficult to interpret and their relationship to paleomagnetic studies have been discussed by a number of authors (FAHRIG and JONES, 1969; IRVING et al., 1972). Fold tests conducted on both natural and demagnetized rock types generally lead to smaller angle of dispersion after correction for tilt (Tables 1 and 2). This tilt correction was applied using individual and local structural rotations taken fro

ancient equator. Gypsum was found in the sedimentary sequences inter- layered with the extrusive rocks of the region (Dr. E. Dimroth, personal com- munication). 13. Discussion of the Results The initial directions of magnetization are scattered, but the scattering is reduced by magnetic cleaning in a peak field of 250 Oe. The scattering is at- tributed to temporary components acquired in the laboratory, viscous compo- nents acquired in the Earth's magnetic field, a fraction of chemical magnetiza- tion, secular variation during the initial cooling and measuring errors. A very high proportion of the opaque minerals are small to medium sized magnetite crystals which are considered to dominate the magnetic properties of the rocks. Minute quantities of hemo-ilmenite are occasionally present. Many sites (6 or 7) yielded mixed polarities but the preponderance of normal polarities is sig- nificant, the reversed magnetization is thought to reflect a reversed ambient field at the time of intrusion. The paleolatitude at the time of intrusion of these rocks was close to the equator suggesting a warm climate in late Aphebian time. The paleopole obtained does not compare with the sequence of apparent polar wan- dering for the interval 2, 100 to 1, 300 m. y. established by MCGLYNN et al. (1974).

Dimroth, personal com- munication). 13. Discussion of the Results The initial directions of magnetization are scattered, but the scattering is reduced by magnetic cleaning in a peak field of 250 Oe. The scattering is at- tributed to temporary components acquired in the laboratory, viscous compo- nents acquired in the Earth's magnetic field, a fraction of chemical magnetiza- tion, secular variation during the initial cooling and measuring errors. A very high proportion of the opaque minerals are small to medium sized magnetite crystals which are considered to dominate the magnetic properties of the rocks. Minute quantities of hemo-ilmenite are occasionally present. Many sites (6 or 7) yielded mixed polarities but the preponderance of normal polarities is sig- nificant, the reversed magnetization is thought to reflect a reversed ambient field at the time of intrusion. The paleolatitude at the time of intrusion of these rocks was close to the equator suggesting a warm climate in late Aphebian time. The paleopole obtained does not compare with the sequence of apparent polar wan- dering for the interval 2, 100 to 1, 300 m. y. established by MCGLYNN et al. (1974).

Introduction This study is centered on the paleomagnetism of the basic intrusive and ex- trusive rocks of the central eastern portion of the Labrador geosyncline. The dispersion of the pole is still relatively large after AF cleaning. Palcomagnetic studies of the Hawaiian Islands have been of primary interest in determining the long-term nature of geomagnetic secular variation in the central Pacific, because the secular variation (SV) is now anomalously low in this region [Fisk, 1931] and because the nondipole part of the geomagnetic field whose changes produce part of the SV is essentially missing [Cox, 1962; Creer, 1962; Doell and Cox, 1971, 1972]. Although the collections are more re- stricted than those previously made on the main islands, they are of some interest in that they extend the mid-Pacific palcomagnetic coverage farther west. Niihau lies about 27 km SW of Kauai. CONCLUSION In summary, the palcomagnetic data from the Kayenta and Summerville formations indicate that the major movement of North America with respect to the pole did not begin until Upper Jurassic (post-Summerville) time. More- over, the palcomagnetic data for North America indicate that two distinct episodes of drift have taken place, one in Upper Jurassic to Creta- ceous times and one in the Upper Cretaceous and Tertiary. These are reflected in the opening of the central Atlantic and the North and central Atlantic, respectively, and are corn- JURASSIC POLAR MOVEMENT pletely compatible with and reinforced by the sea-floor spreading data. Comparison of the sea-floor spreading data, the paleomagnetic record, and the geology of the Atlantic basin as deduced from the Joides drill- ing all suggest that rifting is a two-stage proc- ess involving early initial rifting with little spreading, perhaps extending over a consider- able period of time (Upper Triassic to Upper Jurassic in the case of the Atlantic), followed by a period of rapid spreading in which the major portion of the ocean basin is formed in a relatively short period of time. DISPERSION OF DIRECTIONS AND POLES Directions of remanent magnetization at dif- ferent sites within a single rock body always show a certain amount of scatter; part of this scatter is related to experimental difficulties of many sorts (Creer [1962] provides a short summary), but the rest reflects actual disper- sion of the ancient geomagnetic field. Under favorable circumstances, experimental error can be reduced to insignificant levels, as in the present study, by careful selection of sampling BECK, JR. sites, the use of systematic magnetic cleaning, and by applying fairly exacting rejection cri- teria. Probably the only major experimental source of dispersion contributing to the scatter of directions in the present study is error in selecting the proper tectonic correction. Even here, however, errors are likely to be of the order of 5 ø or less and randomly directed. Under favorable circumstances, experimental error can be reduced to insignificant levels, as in the present study, by careful selection of sampling BECK, JR. sites, the use of systematic magnetic cleaning, and by applying fairly exacting rejection cri- teria. A volcanological sketch map of the region reviewing the esti- mated ages of volcanism in the Ethiopian rift and plateaus has been published [Mohr, 1971]. Generally the youngest volcanics are found in the Afar region and along the central axis of the rift valley, the older volcanics being exposed in the plateau areas. Because of the rapid development of lateritic soil in this region, fresh rock is exposed almost exclusively along relatively recent road excava- tions. Consequently, the most efficient manner of locating and collecting dike samples is to practice armchair geology from a Land Rover. Therefore all the sampled dike localities are situated either along or within 0.5 km of the major road system (Figure 1). each sample was oriented by marking a horizontal plane on the sample. This orientation was determined by a bubble level mounted on a brass plate. carrier_significance_candidates.excerpt: The granitic rocks sampled in this study showed a wide variation in magnetic stability, and therefore it was necessary to analyze every specimen for stability. By using the saturation IRM experiments proposed by Lowrie and Fuller [1971], we found that large values of the ratio Qy in our samples characterize speci- mens with magnetism dominated by single- domain behavior, whereas specimens with low Qd ratios are dominated by grains with multi- domain behavior. If susceptibility x is a mea- sure of the amount of magnetism with very low coercivities (less than 0.45 oe) and the mag- netic intensity J is the measure of grains with coercivities greater than the cleaning level, the ratio J/x would indicate the relative pro- portion of hard and soft fractions. Thus the success of Qd as a stability criterion for our granitic samples from the Central Cascades may be a result of its ability to distinguish the relative proportion of high and low co- ercive magnetic components. Preliminary studies of granitic rocks from the Idaho batholith indicated that the Qd criterion was highly reliable for distinguishing unstable samples, whereas studies of andesRes from the southern San Juan Mountains in south central Colorado showed that Qa' was not a sensitive indicator of stability for these rocks. Therefore the data available at this time would seem to indicate that the Qa' value may not be a universal criterion for all rock types.

the NW-SE trend of the Coast Mountains. They are up to 80 or more kilometers long and up to 30 or so kilometers wide. They commonly grade in composition from basic or intermediate at their perimeters to acidic in the cores (Figure 2). The perimeter phase is most commonly diorite, which is often well foliated or gneissic and may have asso- ciated gabbroic zones. Progressing inward, the plutons grade to quartz diorite and then to granodiorite and finally to quartz monzonite in the core. During this gradation the rocks become increasingly massive or less foliated, and hornblende gives way to biotite as the dominant mafic mineral. The petrography and structure of these plutons have been sum- marized by Hutchison [1970]. Of the four plutons sampled in this study, three come from the eastern age zone. Disadvantages of red bed study are that (1) many time intervals worth studying are not represented by good red bed sections and (2) many red bed sections are unfoSsiliferous or contain fossils that are such poor temporal indicators that the sections can only be dated on the basis of stratigraphic relationships. Because of these limitations it is desirable to extend such studies to nonred sediments, which form the bulk of the sedimentary record and which (particularly for the case of limestones and shales) often contain abundant microfossils allowing more precise dating. Intensive paleomagnetic studies of limestone and shale sec- tions are rare mainly because intensities of magnetization are generally so low (10 -8 emu/cm 3 or lower) that they can only be measured with considerable difficulty [Strangway and McMahon, 1973]. A general location map is shown in Figure 1. The site coordinates are 71ø44'N, 23ø25'W. The samples were collected from the lower middle portion of the Malmros klint member of the Fleming Fjord (formerly Cape Biot) forma- tion, the top of the core being located very roughly 75 m above the base of the member. It was originally planned to drill down to the base of the Malmros klint member and thus acquire a reversal sequence covering a substantial portion of, if not all of, Carnian time, but the threat of early snow forced a halt to drilling. This paper reports the results of 1200 measurements on 208 specimens cut from 134 individually oriented samples from that core. GEOLOGY The Malmros klint member of the Fleming Fjord forma- tion (formerly the Fleming Fjord member of the Cape Biot formation [Perch-Nielsen et al., 1972]) is the middle member of the formation. It is overlain by the Oersted Dal member, a series of mudstones, sandstones, and arkosic conglomerates topped by limestone, dolomite, and a bone bed of Rhetic age. It is underlain by the Edderfugledal member, a siltstone with stromatolitic and oolitic layers [Perch-Nielsen et al., 1972].

the Oersted Dal records a period of Fluvial deposition [Surlyk et al., 1971] and return to marine evapor. itic conditions. The Malmros klint member is approximately 200 m thick in the area of Cape Biot and thins westward, being somewhat thinner in the study area. The intrusion of dolerite sills and dikes during the Tertiary is an important factor in the discussion of the red bed magnetics. The sills are most typically emplaced between Oersted Dal and Kap Stewart. Although these intrusions show little evidence of contact metamorphism, their emplace- ment almost certainly raised regional temperatures enough to add small amounts of fairly stable low-temperature sec- ondary thermal or viscous remanent magnetizations to the original remanence. Comparison of Tarling's [1966] studies and pole positions for the Tertiary igneous rocks with our results from this study leads us to believe that the pole published by Bidgood and Hadand [1961] for the Cape Biot (Fleming Fjord) formation actually records a Tertiary, not a Triassic, field direction. This technique consists of picking the samples from streaked data in groups on the basis of their position in the original NRM distribution. Because no initial streak was present, this selection has instead been made on the 550øC demagnetized sample data. In theory, Helsley's method rests on the assumption that those samples closest to the expected pole position at (or near) the end of the NRM streak will be the most stable and more likely to give true field directions in comparison with those at the opposite end of the streak, which have probably acquired at least some stable components in the secondary direction. In this paper we have followed a similar if somewhat less esthetic course in assuming that those samples nearest the ex- pected direction at the 550øC demagnetization step have the strongest primary magnetizations and are therefore the most likely to yield true directions at the higher demagnetization steps. We have therefore arbitrarily chosen to use only the high-temperature demagnetizations of those samples that had reached the negative third quadrant by 550øC in order to calculate a pole position. The Morin complex is an intrusive mass situated in the Grenville structural province about 50 km north of Montreal. Its situation within the Grenville province and the com- parison of paleomagnetic results from it and other Grenville rocks are described in the companion paper [Irving et al., 1974]. The Grenville province is the youngest and most south- easterly element of the Precambrian shield of Nort, h America, and it consists largely of highly metamorphosed rocks, which have been heated to temperatures in excess of the maximum blocking temperatures of magnetite (580øC) and hematite (675øC), so that any earlier magnetic record was erased. Hence the problems are different from those in conventional paleo- magnetic work, in which rocks are assumed to have acquired their stable magnetization at or soon after deposition. Instead, the magnetization was acquired sometime after regional meta- morphism. Hence there are serious problems in estimating the age of the magnetization. Further problems are the possible effects of anisotropy and the difficulties in assessing relative block rotation within such geologically complex terrain and hence in knowing the horizontal plane at the time

INTRODUCTION Poles computed for the igneous rocks of the Serra Geral [Creer, 1962] and the Vulcanitas Cerro Colorado for- mations [Valencio, 1972] are the only paleomagnetic poles of Lower Cretaceous age available for South America. Paleo- magnetic poles for the Cretaceous La Teta lava [McDonald and Opdyke, 1972] and the Late Cretaceous Poqos de Caldas alkaline complex [Opdyke and McDonald, 1973] have also been reported. Paleomagnetic reconstructions of the ancient relative positions of continents should be based o

cal age for Africa has suggested that the fragmentation of the South American-African block and the origin of the South Atlantic Ocean occurred before the Lower Cretaceous [Creer, 1962; Valencio, 1972] but after the Middle Jurassic [Creer et al., 1972]. More Cretaceous paleomagnetic poles for South America are necessary to sup- port this interpretation. Evidence for the South Atlantic from magnetic anomaly studi es [Heirtzler et al., 1968; Ladd et al., 1975] and from the Deep-Sea Drilling Project [Maxwell et al., 1970] suggests that the South Atlantic had opened to about one half of its present width by the Cretaceous times. Trachybasaltic dikes crop out at Rio de Los Molinos, in the southern part of the Sierra Chica geologic unit of C6rdoba province, Republic of Argentina. Gordillo and Lencinas [1969] have suggested a Lower Cretaceous age for these trachybasaltic dikes. However, a younger K-Ar age (60 4- 3 m.y.) has been obtained for one of the dikes of Rio de Los Molinos. This age is questioned on the grounds that it may have been reset [Gordillo and Lencinas, 1969]. Conclusions The upper Precambrian Port Askaid Tillite of the Dalradian Supergroup of Scotland retains a stable secondary prefolding remanence acquired during Ordovician time as shown by the conglomerate test and by the location of the tilt-corrected clast and matrix pole positions. This conclusion is supported by AF and thermal demagnetisation studies, and by polished and thin section observations which show that the remanen- ce resides in secondary hematite derived from partially to completely altered magnetite. The results support the con- cept that the tillite was likely to have been deposited at mid to high palaeolatitudes during the late Precambrian. The unit then drifted into equatorial palaeolatitudes where it was chemically remagnetizated during the onset of the orogenic activity in Lower Ordovician time by regional burial meta- morphism. Finally the tillite was tilted in Silurian or later time, probably as terminal orogenic event. This method employs one direction of remanent magnetism from each core following demagnetization treatment, the particular alternating field value used being selected so that the minimum scatter of within-lava directions (or maximum Ka is produced. This method of computation is preferred to the more commonly applied single demagnetization treatment for a whole sequence of lavas, or for a series of specimens from a single lava, since several studies show that within- lava magnetic stability can vary greatly, so that different demagnetization treatments are required to minimize unstable components within a single lava. This method employs one direction of remanent magnetism from each core following demagnetization treatment, the particular alternating field value used being selected so that the minimum scatter of within-lava directions (or maximum Ka is produced. This method of computation is preferred to the more commonly applied single demagnetization treatment for a whole sequence of lavas, or for a series of specimens from a single lava, since several studies show that within- lava magnetic stability can vary greatly, so that different demagnetization treatments are required to minimize unstable components within a single lava. This method employs one direction of remanent magnetism from each core following demagnetization treatment, the particular alternating field value used being selected so that the minimum scatter of within-lava directions (or maximum Ka is produced. This method of computation is preferred to the more commonly applied single demagnetization treatment for a whole sequence of lavas, or for a series of specimens from a single lava, since several studies show that within- lava magnetic stability can vary greatly, so that different demagnetization treatments are required to minimize unstable components within a single lava. Such a com- putation leads, in practice, to the effective ' weighting ' of mean directions in single lavas, to the directions of the more stable specimens, which is clearly desirable in Downloaded from https://academic.oup.com/gji/article/28/1/1/630530 by Curtin University Library user on 06 May 2026 Geomagnetic secular variation 15 practice. This computation method has been criticized by Storetvedt (1970) and Van der Voo (1968,1971) who prefer to use data resulting from single demagnetization treatments. Van der Voo (1971) calls the minimum dispersion method ‘ unrealistic’, while at the same time stressing that stability differences exist within single lavas: these statements would appear to be somewhat incompatible. n Possession island is the largest of the Crozet group. Gunn et al. (1972) have compared the petrography and geochemistry of Possession and East Island. While monzonite and syenite have been identified in outcrops on Possession, the island is otherwise very similar geochemically and geomorphologically to East Island, with a series of horizontal to near horizontal lava flows constituting most of the island's surface. No old basement or sub-basalt unconformity is seen on Possession. Age control on the Crozet Islands is by palaeomagnetic and potassium-argon methods. As will be shown below, all lavas sampled on East Island are of normal polarity. A reversed to normal polarity boundary was detected in the lower parts of three of the sequences sampled on Possession (Morne Rouge, Port Alfred, and Crique de Noel) and this was identified as the Brunhes-Matuyama polarity change (t = 0.69 My) by potassium-argon dating (private communication from Dr A. Major motives were to study the volcanic stratigraphy, polarity time scale, petro- graphy, geochemistry, and palaeomagnetic pole positions. These independent studies have defined the segment of the collection which is Brunhes in age, to provide the essential framework for the analysis reported in this paper. Geological control As Cox (1969) has stressed, the substantial difficulties usually involved in assigning geological ages to a series of igneous rocks are greatly minimized for Brunhes epoch (t = 0 to 0.69 My) materials. Outcrops of this age can easily be distinguished from the older Matuyuma epoch materials using polarity differences. Geomorphological criteria, and very high latitude VGP assist in this identification. Nevertheless, potassium-argon age determinations can increase the confidence of such age assignments. We are presenting a compilation of Brunhes epoch paleomagnetic results from igneous rocks of the Indian and Atlantic Ocean regions. Many of the data have already been presented. We describe below the geological control only for those sampling sites previously unreported. The geographic co-ordinates of each body are included in Table 1. The geological control for the remaining results are given in the respective references. Latitude in degrees. Hemispheres not distinguished. The Comore Islands Four principal islands comprise the Comores, which are located at the northern end of the Mozambique Channel (Fig. 3). Esson et al. (1970) have recently reviewed the geology of the islands. Brunhes epoch lavas have been sampled on Grande Comore and Anjouan. Grande Comore is the largest of the Comore Islands, and is geomorphologically young, being without any deeply incised valleys. It is dominated by the volcanic centres of Massif del a Grille (rising to 1087 metres above sea level) and Le Kartala (2361 metres), in the north and south respectively. Five of the sampled lava flows are from fissures of the northern centre. The possible tectonic significance of sand- stone inclusions in these lavas have been discussed by Strong & Flowers (1969).
